title: The Friend has come home
hook: the Friend has come to my home; the True One brought us together (Suhi M1, ang 764)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one whose head He guards, and your line: guarded. Did you touch your head when fear rose? Today, a hymn of arrival, sung on the morning of many Sikh weddings. Day six hundred sixty-one.

The doorbell rings and you already know who it is. Maybe a brother back from deployment, a daughter home from her first semester, an old friend you haven't seen in ten years. You open the door and the whole house changes. The air feels different. Somebody starts cooking. Guru Nanak wrote a hymn for exactly that feeling, the instant the one you've waited for crosses the threshold. And Sikhs sing it on one of the biggest mornings of a life.
screen: `THE DOORBELL RINGS.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE CHANGES.` → `A HYMN FOR THE THRESHOLD.`

segments.voice: The hymn is a chhant, a longer song form, in Raag Suhi, on ang 764. It opens, in effect: the friend has come to my home; the True One has brought about this meeting. Then: the meeting came naturally, pleasing to the Lord's mind; I've found what my heart was set on. Night and day there is union, my mind is content, my home and temple are made beautiful. The unstruck music plays. The friend has come to my home. The word is saajan: friend, beloved, the dear one. In Punjabi the verb can carry the friend or the friends, and Sikhs hear both. On the surface, guests arriving for a celebration, the house filling up. Underneath, the Beloved, the One, arriving in the heart. Raag Suhi is associated with weddings and with joy, and this chhant is often sung in the gurdwara at the start of a Sikh wedding, before the couple walks the lavan. You can see why. A family's home fills with friends. Two people are brought together, and the hymn says plainly who did it: the True One made the meeting. And beneath it all, the Sikh image of every soul as a bride waiting for the Beloved to come home. Notice the order in the hymn: the arrival first, and then the house becomes beautiful. Not the other way around. Nobody has to make their home perfect before the friend can come. It's the coming that makes it beautiful. Tomorrow, the first of those four wedding rounds.
screen: `SAAJAN: FRIEND, BELOVED.` · `THE TRUE ONE MADE THE MEETING.` · `SUNG AS A WEDDING BEGINS.` · `THE COMING MAKES THE HOUSE BEAUTIFUL.` · then, large: `THE FRIEND IS HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Picture your own front door. Picture someone you love walking through it: someone who's coming soon, or someone you wish would. See their face as the door opens. Feel what changes in the room, and in you. Let that joy be as big as it wants. Then, if you pray, you can welcome the One the same way, with a quiet Waheguru, as if the One were the friend at the door. If you don't, simply rest in the welcome. The bell holds the time.
The Friend has come home. Guru Nanak's wedding chhant: the friend has come to my home, the True One made the meeting, and the house is made beautiful.
screen: `THE FRIEND HAS COME HOME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the friend is home. Today, welcome someone home properly: get up, go to the door, and greet them like you've been waiting. Day six hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Suhi chhant 'ham ghar saajan aae' in kirtan, and it is often sung at the start of the Anand Karaj, the wedding, before the lavan.

original.note: Gurmukhi: friend, beloved; ham ghar saajan aae, the friend has come to my home.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song about guests arriving.
what it means: guests and the Beloved at once: the True One makes the meeting and the house becomes beautiful.
what a scholar hears: the Suhi chhant uses bridal imagery for the soul's union with the One; anahad shabad, the unstruck music, marks it as mystical union as well as celebration.
